questions.question_text: Which of the following represents a fundamental difference between analytical and descriptive studies?

options.text: Analytical studies describe group characteristics while descriptive studies make comparisons
Analytical studies involve comparative analysis of groups; descriptive studies have no comparison
Descriptive studies are always prospective
Analytical studies cannot be used for rare diseases
Descriptive studies always use experimental designs

correct_answer.text: Analytical studies involve comparative analysis of groups; descriptive studies have no comparison

questions.explanation: Analytical studies involve comparative analysis of two groups to measure the association between variables, while descriptive studies describe the characteristics present in members of the study group with no testing of a causal hypothesis or any comparisons with other groups. Option A reverses this. Options C, D, E are incorrect.

questions.question_text: An interventional study randomly assigns depressed patients to either cognitive-behavioral therapy or a waitlist control condition. Why is randomization important for this research question?

options.text: Randomization ensures all participants will recover from depression
Randomization distributes confounding variables between groups, supporting causal inference about treatment effect
Randomization eliminates the need for follow-up outcome measurement
Randomization is only necessary for observational, not experimental, studies
Randomization prevents all recall bias in outcome reporting

correct_answer.text: Randomization distributes confounding variables between groups, supporting causal inference about treatment effect

questions.explanation: Randomization balances both measured and unmeasured confounders between treatment and control groups, allowing researchers to attribute outcome differences to the intervention rather than other factors. This supports causal inference. Options A, C, D, and E either overstate randomization's effects or misstate when it applies. ---

questions.question_text: What is the main advantage of prospective longitudinal studies compared to retrospective case-control studies in studying risk factors?

options.text: Longitudinal studies are less expensive
Longitudinal studies directly measure incidence and can establish clear temporal relationships
Longitudinal studies eliminate the need for a control group
Longitudinal studies automatically prevent all confounding
Longitudinal studies can only be used for common diseases

correct_answer.text: Longitudinal studies directly measure incidence and can establish clear temporal relationships

questions.explanation: Prospective longitudinal studies follow subjects forward from baseline, clearly establishing that exposure precedes outcome (temporal sequence), and directly measure incidence rates. Case-control studies have difficulty establishing temporality retrospectively. Option A is false—longitudinal studies are costly and time-consuming. Option C is incorrect. Options D and E misstate design characteristics. ---

questions.question_text: What is the main reason longitudinal studies are less commonly used than case-control studies in preliminary investigations of risk factors?

options.text: Longitudinal studies cannot measure risk factors
Longitudinal studies are costly and time-consuming
Longitudinal studies always require randomization
Longitudinal studies cannot recruit adequate controls
Longitudinal studies are unsuitable for psychiatric research

correct_answer.text: Longitudinal studies are costly and time-consuming

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states But longitudinal studies are costly and time-consuming, explaining why case-control studies are often the first approach despite their limitations. Options A, C, D, E are incorrect statements about longitudinal studies.

questions.question_text: In case-control studies, the maximum ratio of controls to cases that improves study power is approximately:
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states up to a ratio of 4:1, when the number of controls is increased, the power of a study increases. But not after exceeding this ratio. This is a direct factual recall. Options A, B, C represent suboptimal ratios, and Option E exceeds the effective limit.

questions.question_text: A researcher is designing a study to examine whether maternal stress during pregnancy is associated with autism spectrum disorder in offspring. Which design would provide the strongest evidence for causality?

options.text: Case-control study starting with diagnosed autism cases
Cross-sectional study comparing stress levels and autism diagnosis
Prospective cohort study following pregnant women and tracking autism outcomes
Ecological study examining regional stress and autism rates
Case reports of maternal stress and autism

correct_answer.text: Prospective cohort study following pregnant women and tracking autism outcomes

questions.explanation: A prospective cohort study would establish temporality (exposure before outcome), measure incidence, and allow for comparison of risk between exposed and non-exposed groups. Option A lacks temporality. Option B cannot establish causality cross-sectionally. Option D risks ecological fallacy. Option E is descriptive only.

questions.question_text: Why might a researcher choose neighborhood controls rather than hospital-based controls in a case-control study?

options.text: Neighborhood controls are always cheaper to recruit
Neighborhood controls are more likely to represent the general population from which cases were drawn
Neighborhood controls automatically eliminate matching requirements
Neighborhood controls prevent all selection bias
Neighborhood controls can measure relative risk directly

correct_answer.text: Neighborhood controls are more likely to represent the general population from which cases were drawn

questions.explanation: Neighborhood controls are population-based and typically share similar background characteristics and exposure opportunities as cases drawn from the general population, enhancing representativeness. Hospital-based controls may have different exposure patterns due to their own health conditions or healthcare-seeking behavior. Options A, C, D, and E misstate advantages or make false claims. ---

questions.question_text: Which aspect of case definition is most critical in a case-control study investigating a psychiatric disorder?

options.text: Cases must be younger than 40 years old
Strict diagnostic criteria must be followed to ensure valid case identification
Cases must have suffered from the disorder for at least 5 years
All cases must be recruited from hospital settings
Cases must have a positive family history of the disorder

correct_answer.text: Strict diagnostic criteria must be followed to ensure valid case identification

questions.explanation: Evidence emphasizes that defining a case is crucial—strict diagnostic criteria and eligibility criteria must be followed. Valid case identification is fundamental to the study's validity. Options A, C, D, and E are arbitrary constraints that are not universally necessary. ---

questions.question_text: In describing the natural course of illness and identifying risk factors, which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Cross-sectional survey
Case-control study
Prospective longitudinal study
Ecological study
Experimental trial

correct_answer.text: Prospective longitudinal study

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that In prospective longitudinal studies, observations are repeated in the same population over a prolonged time. This is helpful to study the natural course of illness, study risk factors and find out incidence rates. Options A, B, D are not designed for this purpose. Option E involves intervention.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist reviews 50 case files of patients who developed neuroleptic malignant syndrome and compares their medication histories to 100 randomly selected patients who did not develop this syndrome. What type of study design is being used?

options.text: Prospective cohort study
Case-control study
Cross-sectional survey
Experimental trial
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Case-control study

questions.explanation: This describes a case-control design: cases (those with neuroleptic malignant syndrome) are identified, controls (those without) are selected, and exposure (medication history) is assessed retrospectively. Options A describes prospective follow-up. Options C, D, E don't match this design.

questions.question_text: In ecological studies examining the correlation between regional antidepressant prescription rates and suicide mortality, why is it problematic to conclude that high antidepressant use causes low suicide at the individual level?

options.text: Ecological studies are always too large to be valid
Drawing subject-level conclusions from group-level data represents ecological fallacy
Suicide is too rare to study at the ecological level
Antidepressants cannot affect suicide rates
Regional data cannot be collected accurately

correct_answer.text: Drawing subject-level conclusions from group-level data represents ecological fallacy

questions.explanation: This directly describes ecological fallacy—drawing subject-level conclusions from group-level observations. The regional association tells nothing about which individuals receive antidepressants or commit suicide. Option A is incorrect. Option C contradicts study feasibility. Option D is factually wrong. Option E doesn't address the logical fallacy.

questions.question_text: Which feature of descriptive studies best explains why they cannot test a causal hypothesis?

options.text: They lack a control group for comparison
They do not involve manipulation of variables
They cannot measure both exposure and outcome
They only include exposed subjects
They always have small sample sizes

correct_answer.text: They lack a control group for comparison

questions.explanation: Descriptive studies by definition have no testing of a causal hypothesis or any comparisons with other groups, which requires a control group. Causality requires comparative analysis between groups. Option B is true but doesn't explain the lack of causal hypothesis testing. Options C, D, E are not accurate characteristic of descriptive studies.

questions.question_text: A case-control study investigates whether antipsychotic medication is associated with metabolic syndrome. Cases have metabolic syndrome; controls do not. Cases are recruited from endocrinology clinics while controls are recruited from the general population. What potential problem does this introduce?

options.text: The study cannot measure odds ratio
Selection bias may occur if antipsychotic use differs between clinic and community populations
Recall bias is eliminated by using clinic-based cases
The study becomes prospective rather than retrospective
Matching becomes impossible to perform

correct_answer.text: Selection bias may occur if antipsychotic use differs between clinic and community populations

questions.explanation: Recruiting cases and controls from different sources (clinic vs. community) may introduce selection bias because antipsychotic use patterns differ between these populations. Cases from metabolic clinics may have different medication histories than community controls, confounding the exposure-outcome relationship. Options A is false (odds ratio can still be measured). Option C misunderstands bias direction. Options D and E incorrectly describe the design consequences. ---

questions.question_text: A depression registry follows 2,000 patients diagnosed with major depression for 5 years, measuring recovery rates and symptom trajectories. This is best described as which type of study?

options.text: Case-control study
Cross-sectional study
Prospective longitudinal cohort study
Experimental trial
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Prospective longitudinal cohort study

questions.explanation: Prospective longitudinal studies are described as studies where observations are repeated in the same population over a prolonged time, helpful to study natural course of illness. The 5-year follow-up with repeated measures matches this definition. Options A, B, E are descriptive/analytical but not longitudinal. Option D requires intervention.

questions.question_text: A case-control study examining risk factors for bipolar disorder cannot directly measure which epidemiological parameter?

options.text: Odds ratio of exposure among cases versus controls
Incidence rate of bipolar disorder
Proportion of cases exposed to a risk factor
Proportion of controls exposed to a risk factor
Association between exposure and disease

correct_answer.text: Incidence rate of bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Incidence cannot be measured—so odds ratio only—not relative risk—can be measured in case-control studies. Because incidence requires knowing the number of new cases in a population at risk, case-control studies cannot measure it. Options A, C, D, E are all measurable in case-control designs.

questions.question_text: Which type of descriptive study provides information about the characteristics of an entire population rather than a subset?

options.text: Case report
Case series
Survey
Census
Ecological study

correct_answer.text: Census

questions.explanation: A census is explicitly described as a special cross-sectional study that includes the whole population rather than a sample subset. This distinguishes it from surveys and other cross-sectional studies. Options A and B are case-based descriptive studies. Option C is a sample-based cross-sectional survey. Option E is analytical, not descriptive in the traditional sense. ---

questions.question_text: How does overzealous matching in a case-control study affect the study's ability to detect an association between exposure and disease?

options.text: It increases statistical power indefinitely
It may reduce the observed difference between exposure rates in cases and controls
It eliminates confounding variables entirely
It prevents selection bias from occurring
It ensures that all matched variables are causal factors

correct_answer.text: It may reduce the observed difference between exposure rates in cases and controls

questions.explanation: Excessive matching can inadvertently match on causal factors themselves, reducing the contrast between cases and controls on the exposure of interest, thus obscuring the true association. The source explicitly warns that overzealous matching may inadvertently result in matching for putative causal factors. Options A, C, D, and E overstate the benefits or incorrectly describe matching effects. ---

questions.question_text: A case-control study examining antidepressant use and the risk of suicidal ideation in adolescents finds a higher proportion of antidepressant exposure among cases (adolescents with suicidal ideation) compared to controls. What is the most important limitation of concluding that antidepressants cause suicidal ideation?

options.text: The study did not measure incidence rates
Temporality is difficult to determine retrospectively in case-control studies
The study used hospital controls instead of population controls
The matching procedure was inadequate
The sample size was too small

correct_answer.text: Temporality is difficult to determine retrospectively in case-control studies

questions.explanation: A critical limitation is that with retrospective data collection, it's unclear whether antidepressant use preceded or followed the emergence of suicidal ideation. The source explicitly identifies this as a major disadvantage: Temporality is difficult to determine retrospectively. Option A is a limitation but doesn't directly address causality. Options C, D, E are methodological issues but not the core limitation for causality in this scenario.

questions.question_text: Which clinical inquiry is best answered using a pragmatic randomized controlled trial rather than an explanatory RCT?

options.text: What is the efficacy of this new antipsychotic under ideal conditions?
What is the effectiveness of this antidepressant in routine clinical practice?
What is the mechanism of action of this mood stabilizer?
What is the diagnostic accuracy of this new assessment tool?
What is the cost per quality-adjusted life year of this intervention?

correct_answer.text: What is the effectiveness of this antidepressant in routine clinical practice?

questions.explanation: Pragmatic RCTs measure treatment effectiveness in real-world clinical settings, answering whether an intervention works in practice. Explanatory (experimental) RCTs measure efficacy under controlled conditions. Option A describes explanatory RCT goals. Options C and D require different designs (mechanistic study and diagnostic accuracy). Option E is health economics but not the defining distinction between pragmatic and explanatory approaches. ---

questions.question_text: Why can case-control studies measure several different risk factors for a single disease outcome more efficiently than cohort studies?

options.text: Case-control studies eliminate confounding variables completely
Cases with the disease are already identified, avoiding lengthy follow-up
Controls can be perfectly matched on all relevant variables
Case-control studies measure absolute risk rather than relative risk
Selection bias is less problematic in case-control designs

correct_answer.text: Cases with the disease are already identified, avoiding lengthy follow-up

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are efficient for studying multiple exposures because the outcome (disease) has already occurred – researchers can rapidly assemble cases and retrospectively assess multiple exposures without waiting for disease development, unlike time-consuming prospective cohort studies.

questions.question_text: What is the key difference between prospective and retrospective research designs?

options.text: Prospective studies measure prevalence while retrospective studies measure incidence
Prospective studies follow subjects forward from exposure to outcome; retrospective studies look backward from outcome to exposure
Retrospective studies are always more accurate than prospective studies
Prospective designs are unsuitable for psychiatric research
Prospective studies cannot use control groups

correct_answer.text: Prospective studies follow subjects forward from exposure to outcome; retrospective studies look backward from outcome to exposure

questions.explanation: The distinction clearly: whether the study looks forward (prospective) from the exposure to the outcome, or backwards (retrospective) from the outcome to the exposure. Option A incorrectly reverses the relationship with prevalence/incidence. Options C, D, and E are incorrect generalizations.

questions.question_text: A researcher studying rare psychiatric conditions is deciding between a case-control study and a cohort study. Which design is more suitable?

options.text: Cohort study, because it measures relative risk
Case-control study, because it is suitable for investigating rare diseases
Ecological study, because it avoids selection bias
Cross-sectional study, because it requires less time
Experimental study, because it provides the strongest evidence

correct_answer.text: Case-control study, because it is suitable for investigating rare diseases

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are specifically described as suitable for investigating rare diseases because they start with identified cases. Cohort studies are inefficient for rare outcomes (require very large samples). Option A is incorrect on design choice. Options C and D don't address rarity of disease. Option E (experimental) isn't indicated for descriptive epidemiology of rare conditions.

questions.question_text: A study examines countries with varying rates of religious attachment and finds that nations with low religious attachment have high suicide rates. The researchers conclude that low religious attachment causes suicide. What is this reasoning error called?

options.text: Selection bias
Recall bias
Ecological fallacy
Confounding bias
Attrition bias

correct_answer.text: Ecological fallacy

questions.explanation: Ecological fallacy occurs when group-level associations are assumed to apply to individuals within those groups. The finding that countries with low religious attachment have high suicide rates says nothing about whether the individuals committing suicide in those countries are themselves non-religious. This is the textbook definition of ecological fallacy provided in the source. Options A and B relate to case-control biases. Options D and E are other bias types but not applicable to this error. ---

questions.question_text: When recruiting multiple controls per case in a case-control study, what is the practical limit to increasing the control:case ratio?

options.text: 1:1 is optimal; higher ratios add no benefit
2:1 is the maximum recommended ratio
Up to 4:1 improves power; beyond this there is minimal additional benefit
Ratios should always exceed 4:1 for statistical power
There is no limit; more controls always increase power

correct_answer.text: Up to 4:1 improves power; beyond this there is minimal additional benefit

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Up to a ratio of 4:1, when the number of controls is increased, the power of a study increases. But not after exceeding this ratio. This defines the practical limit. Options A, B are suboptimal. Options D, E incorrectly suggest higher ratios always improve power.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study, cases and controls must be identical in all respects except for which variable?

options.text: Age and sex
Presence or absence of the disease being studied
Exposure history to the risk factor of interest
Socioeconomic status
Geographical location

correct_answer.text: Presence or absence of the disease being studied

questions.explanation: By definition, controls differ from cases only in that they do not have the disease being investigated. Controls must be comparable to cases in all other relevant aspects but must be recruited independently of exposure status and disease-free. Options A, D, and E may be matched but are not the defining criterion. Option C is explicitly incorrect—controls should differ in exposure status; this is what the study measures. ---

questions.question_text: What is the primary defining characteristic that distinguishes a case-control study from a cohort study?

options.text: Case-control studies are prospective while cohort studies are retrospective
Case-control studies start from outcome status while cohort studies start from exposure status
Case-control studies measure relative risk while cohort studies measure odds ratio
Case-control studies require larger sample sizes than cohort studies
Case-control studies can only be used for rare diseases while cohort studies cannot

correct_answer.text: Case-control studies start from outcome status while cohort studies start from exposure status

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are retrospective designs that begin by identifying cases (with disease) and controls (without disease), then look back at exposure history. Cohort studies are prospective, starting with exposed and non-exposed groups and following them forward to measure outcomes. The starting point (outcome vs. exposure) is the fundamental structural difference. Option A is reversed. Option C is backwards—cohort studies measure relative risk and case-control studies measure odds ratio. Options D and E misrepresent design flexibility. ---

questions.question_text: A cross-sectional survey is conducted to determine the proportion of a psychiatric patient population experiencing medication side effects at a single point in time. What is the primary limitation of using this design to establish causality?

options.text: The study population is too small to detect associations
Exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously, making temporal sequence unclear
Cross-sectional designs inherently suffer from complete loss to follow-up
The design requires matching of all demographic variables
The study cannot include any control group for comparison

correct_answer.text: Exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously, making temporal sequence unclear

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies capture a snapshot at one point in time, measuring both exposure and outcome together. This simultaneous measurement makes it impossible to determine which came first—a core requirement for establishing causality. Options A and C mischaracterize design limitations. Option D confuses case-control matching with cross-sectional requirements. Option E is false—cross-sectional studies can include comparisons. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher plans to match cases and controls on age and sex in a case-control study. Which statement best describes a potential consequence of this matching strategy?

options.text: Matching will increase the statistical power of the study indefinitely
Overzealous matching may inadvertently match for causal factors, reducing observed associations
Matching eliminates all selection bias from the study design
Matching ensures that age and sex cannot be confounders in the analysis
Matching is required before any case-control study can proceed ethically

correct_answer.text: Overzealous matching may inadvertently match for causal factors, reducing observed associations

questions.explanation: While appropriate matching improves comparability, excessive matching on too many variables risks matching on unmeasured causal factors themselves, which would reduce or obscure the true association between exposure and disease. This is explicitly noted in the source material. Option A is false—benefits plateau and matching increases complexity. Option C overstates the effect; matching addresses comparability, not selection bias per se. Option D is incorrect—matched variables require adjusted analysis. Option E incorrectly states matching is ethically mandatory. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher recruits hospital patients with different conditions as controls for a psychiatric case-control study. Which characteristic must these hospital controls have?

options.text: The same socioeconomic status as cases
The same psychiatric symptoms as cases
A different health problem to the one studied
Previous exposure to the putative risk factor
Matching on all demographic variables

correct_answer.text: A different health problem to the one studied

questions.explanation: Controls can be hospital patients who have a different health problem to the one studied. Option B would contaminate the control group. Option A is one possible matching variable, not a requirement. Option D contradicts the need for controls to be independent of exposure status. Option E represents overzealous matching.

questions.question_text: A case-control study is best described as which type of research design?

options.text: Experimental and prospective
Observational and retrospective
Descriptive and cross-sectional
Longitudinal and prospective
Interventional and randomized

correct_answer.text: Observational and retrospective

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are retrospective analytical designs where researchers start from defined groups of cases and controls, then collect retrospective data on exposure. They are observational (not experimental) because no deliberate manipulation of exposure occurs. Options A and E describe experimental/interventional studies. Option C describes descriptive or cross-sectional designs. Option D incorrectly suggests prospective timing when case-control is inherently retrospective.

questions.question_text: A study measures the association between smoking and schizophrenia by assessing current smoking status and psychiatric diagnosis in 2,000 individuals on a single day. What major limitation applies to this design?

options.text: The study cannot measure prevalence
Temporal sequence cannot be established because exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously
The study requires excessive matching of variables
Only case-control studies can investigate psychiatric associations
The design inherently proves causation

correct_answer.text: Temporal sequence cannot be established because exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously

questions.explanation: In this cross-sectional snapshot design, both smoking (exposure) and schizophrenia diagnosis (outcome) are measured at the same time. This prevents determination of whether smoking preceded schizophrenia onset or vice versa, making temporal inference impossible. Option A is false—cross-sectional studies measure prevalence. Options C, D, and E mischaracterize the design's properties. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about cross-sectional studies is correct?

options.text: They measure incidence rates of disease
They are also called prevalence studies
They allow determination of temporality between exposure and outcome
They require matching of exposed and non-exposed subjects
They are the gold standard for establishing causality

correct_answer.text: They are also called prevalence studies

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies are explicitly described as prevalence studies that provide a snapshot at a single point in time. They measure associations but not temporality (Option C is incorrect—temporality cannot be established from cross-sectional data). Option A (incidence) requires longitudinal studies. Option D (matching) is a case-control technique. Option E is incorrect—case-control or cohort studies are better for causality.

questions.question_text: A study examines the relationship between psychiatric medication use and weight gain by measuring both variables in 500 patients at a single clinic visit. The study can legitimately assess which of the following?

options.text: The temporal relationship between medication initiation and weight gain
The incidence of weight gain in patients starting new medications
The association between current medication use and current weight status in this sample
The relative risk of weight gain attributable to medications
The causal mechanism by which medication causes weight gain

correct_answer.text: The association between current medication use and current weight status in this sample

questions.explanation: A cross-sectional design can assess the association or correlation between variables measured simultaneously. Options A requires temporal sequence (prospective design). Option B requires incidence measurement (cohort design). Option D requires comparative risk calculation in exposed/unexposed cohorts. Option E requires mechanistic investigation beyond this design's scope. ---

questions.question_text: Which methodological feature distinguishes analytical studies from descriptive studies?

options.text: Analytical studies are always prospective while descriptive studies are always retrospective
Analytical studies compare two groups to assess associations while descriptive studies characterize single groups without comparisons
Analytical studies are always more expensive than descriptive studies
Descriptive studies cannot measure any health outcomes
Analytical studies eliminate all potential biases

correct_answer.text: Analytical studies compare two groups to assess associations while descriptive studies characterize single groups without comparisons

questions.explanation: Analytical studies involve comparative analysis of groups to measure associations between variables (exposure/outcome relationships). Descriptive studies characterize and distribute features within a group without testing causal hypotheses or group comparisons. Options A, C, D, and E misstate distinctions or make false claims. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following study designs is specifically used to measure incidence rates and study the natural course of illness?

options.text: Case reports
Cross-sectional surveys
Prospective longitudinal cohort studies
Ecological studies
Case-control studies

correct_answer.text: Prospective longitudinal cohort studies

questions.explanation: Prospective longitudinal studies follow the same population over time, allowing measurement of incidence rates (new cases) and observation of disease progression and natural history. This repeated observation in the same cohort is essential for these purposes. Case reports (A) and ecological studies (E) are descriptive. Cross-sectional studies (B) measure prevalence at one timepoint. Case-control studies (D) measure odds ratio retrospectively and cannot measure incidence. ---

questions.question_text: A nested case-control study is conducted within a larger cohort study. Which advantage does this approach provide over a standalone case-control study?

options.text: It eliminates the need for controls entirely
It provides clear temporal sequence because the cohort was assembled before disease occurred
It prevents matching from occurring
It measures relative risk instead of odds ratio
It automatically ensures no confounding variables exist

correct_answer.text: It provides clear temporal sequence because the cohort was assembled before disease occurred

questions.explanation: A nested case-control study within a cohort benefits from the prospective cohort's temporal clarity—exposure was documented before disease outcome occurred. This strengthens causal inference compared to a standalone retrospective case-control study where temporality is ambiguous. Options A, C, D, and E either incorrectly state design features or overstate benefits. ---

questions.question_text: Which statement best explains why case-control studies cannot directly measure relative risk?

options.text: Controls are too difficult to identify in clinical practice
Incidence rates cannot be calculated when subjects are selected based on outcome status
The researcher cannot follow subjects forward in time
Matching reduces the comparability between groups
Case-control studies are always smaller than cohort studies

correct_answer.text: Incidence rates cannot be calculated when subjects are selected based on outcome status

questions.explanation: Relative risk requires knowing the incidence of disease in exposed versus unexposed populations. Case-control studies select subjects based on disease status (cases vs. controls), making it impossible to calculate true incidence in exposed groups. This is why odds ratio is calculated instead. Options A, C, D, and E either misstate reasons or are factually incorrect about the design's capability. ---

questions.question_text: A cohort study follows 1,000 exposed individuals and 1,000 unexposed individuals over 5 years to measure the development of a psychiatric condition. What does this design directly measure?

options.text: Odds ratio of exposure
Relative risk of the outcome
Prevalence of the exposure
Population attributable risk only
Cross-sectional association strength

correct_answer.text: Relative risk of the outcome

questions.explanation: Cohort studies are prospective designs that follow groups with different exposure status forward to measure outcomes, directly calculating incidence and relative risk (the ratio of incidence in exposed vs. unexposed groups). Case-control studies measure odds ratio (A), not cohort studies. Option C confuses exposure measurement. Option D is incomplete. Option E describes cross-sectional designs, not cohort studies. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key disadvantage of case-control studies?

options.text: They cannot identify multiple etiological factors
Incidence cannot be measured, so only odds ratio can be calculated
They require prolonged follow-up of subjects
They are unsuitable for rare diseases
They measure relative risk rather than odds ratio

correct_answer.text: Incidence cannot be measured, so only odds ratio can be calculated

questions.explanation: The source lists Incidence cannot be measured—so odds ratio only—not relative risk—can be measured as a key disadvantage. Option A is false (multiple factors can be studied). Option C describes cohort studies. Option D is false (case-control is suitable for rare diseases). Option E is backwards—odds ratio is what can be calculated, not relative risk.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the relationship between study design and bias in case-control studies is most accurate?

options.text: Case-control studies are highly prone to selection and recall bias
Case-control studies eliminate bias through matching procedures
Selection bias is impossible in retrospective designs
Recall bias only affects prospective studies
Bias is unrelated to case definition

correct_answer.text: Case-control studies are highly prone to selection and recall bias

questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists Highly prone to selection and recall bias as a disadvantage of case-control studies. Option B is incorrect—matching reduces but doesn't eliminate bias. Option C is false—retrospective designs are particularly vulnerable to bias. Option D is false—recall bias specifically affects retrospective studies. Option E is false—strict case definition helps minimize bias.

questions.question_text: A psychiatric epidemiologist wants to understand the prevalence of anxiety disorders in a specific urban population at a given time. Which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Cohort study
Case-control study
Cross-sectional survey
Prospective longitudinal study
Experimental trial

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional survey

questions.explanation: The clinical enquiry table indicates that determining How common is a condition? requires a cross-sectional study. Cross-sectional studies are described as prevalence studies providing a snapshot at a single point in time. Options A and D are for incidence/risk factors. Option B is for causes (retrospectively). Option E is inappropriate for descriptive prevalence.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study investigating a rare psychiatric disorder, why is this design particularly advantageous?

options.text: It eliminates the need for control group selection
It allows researchers to study rare outcomes efficiently without waiting for disease development
It provides direct measurement of incidence rates in the population
It removes the possibility of temporal bias in exposure assessment
It ensures equal distribution of confounding variables between groups

correct_answer.text: It allows researchers to study rare outcomes efficiently without waiting for disease development

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are specifically suited for rare diseases because researchers can actively recruit affected individuals (cases) rather than waiting for rare events to occur in a prospective study. This makes the design efficient for uncommon conditions. Option A is incorrect—control selection remains essential and challenging. Option C is false—case-control studies cannot measure incidence, only odds ratio. Option D is incorrect—temporal bias remains a significant weakness. Option E overstates the design's protective qualities. ---

questions.question_text: A descriptive study documents clinical features and symptom presentations in 50 patients diagnosed with a novel psychiatric syndrome. What can this study legitimately conclude?

options.text: The syndrome is caused by abnormal dopamine levels
The described characteristics are present in this group of patients
The syndrome is more common in women than men
The disorder is heritable
The described symptoms will improve with antipsychotic medication

correct_answer.text: The described characteristics are present in this group of patients

questions.explanation: Descriptive studies only characterize the distribution of features in a study group without testing causal hypotheses or making comparisons with other groups. They document what is present. Options A, D, and E require analytical or experimental designs. Option C requires comparative analysis (case series lack a comparison group). ---

questions.question_text: According to the source material, what is the primary reason case-control studies are considered often the first mode of studying a suspected association of causality?

options.text: Case-control studies are the only design that can establish causality
Case-control studies are efficient and practical for investigating suspected associations when the disease is rare
Case-control studies are less prone to bias than all other designs
Case-control studies can measure both relative risk and odds ratio simultaneously
Case-control studies are the least expensive design available

correct_answer.text: Case-control studies are efficient and practical for investigating suspected associations when the disease is rare

questions.explanation: Case-control studies allow researchers to directly recruit rare disease cases and compare exposure history, making them efficient first-line investigations when causality is suspected but disease occurrence is uncommon. Evidence shows they are often the first mode and are mostly useful in diseases where exposure is common but the disease occurs only in a small proportion. Options A overstates exclusivity. Option C is false (case-control studies have significant biases). Options D and E misstate design properties.

questions.question_text: How should controls be identified in a case-control study to ensure valid comparisons?

options.text: Controls must have the same exposure status as cases

Controls should always be matched on all sociodemographic variables

Controls must come from hospital settings to ensure availability

questions.question_text: A case-control study of antidepressant use and suicidal behavior finds an odds ratio of 2.5. Which statement correctly interprets this finding?

The odds of antidepressant exposure are 2.5 times higher in cases than controls
Antidepressants prevent suicidal behavior with 60% efficacy
Suicidal behavior is 2.5 times more common in the general population

correct_answer.text: The odds of antidepressant exposure are 2.5 times higher in cases than controls

This is the correct interpretation of odds ratio from case-control studies. Option A overstates and confuses with relative risk. Option B misdefines odds ratio. Option D introduces concepts not measured. Option E misapplies the finding. ---

questions.question_text: A clinical trial testing a new antipsychotic medication in patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is what type of study?

options.text: Descriptive case series
Cohort study
Experimental/interventional study
Ecological study
Case-control study

questions.question_text: Which type of study design should be used to investigate treatment efficacy?

Experimental RCT or systematic reviews
Cohort study
Case-control study
Cross-sectional survey

questions.explanation: The clinical enquiry table specifies that treatment efficacy requires experimental RCT or systematic reviews. Pragmatic RCTs (Option A) are for treatment effectiveness. questions.question_text: In the hierarchy of evidence for psychiatric epidemiology, a systematic review of multiple prospective cohort studies examining risk factors for schizophrenia would rank higher than a single case-control study primarily because:

questions.explanation: Systematic reviews of cohort studies provide stronger evidence because: (1) cohort studies measure incidence and relative risk directly, superior to case-control odds ratios; (2) systematic reviews synthesize multiple studies, reducing random error; (3) prospective designs establish temporality. Option A overstates (bias can exist). Option C is false (case-control is suitable for rare diseases). Option D is false—prospective studies are typically more costly. Option E is incorrect—randomization serves different purposes than systematic reviews.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes why case-control studies are often the first mode of studying a suspected association?

questions.question_text: A longitudinal study following patients with untreated depression finds that 60% develop severe functional impairment over 2 years. What epidemiological measure does this represent?

Cumulative incidence or risk
Odds ratio of functional impairment
Relative risk compared to controls
Ecological correlation between depression and impairment

questions.explanation: The proportion of initially unaffected individuals who develop an outcome (functional impairment) over a specified time period is cumulative incidence or risk. Option A measures existing cases. Option C requires a control group. Option D requires comparison. Option E describes group-level analysis.

questions.question_text: A researcher is undecided between case-control and cohort study designs for examining smoking as a risk factor for depression. Which consideration would particularly favor the case-control approach?

options.text: Case-control studies can measure relative risk directly
Case-control studies require less time and expense
Cohort studies cannot identify multiple risk factors
Case-control studies eliminate selection bias
Case-control studies establish clearer temporal relationships

questions.explanation: The source lists case-control advantages as Easy to carry out, Less time-consuming, and Less expensive. Option A is backwards—cohort studies measure relative risk. questions.question_text: In a case-control study, cases can be obtained from hospital populations or general population. What is a key consideration when selecting cases?

questions.question_text: Why are longitudinal studies described as both costly and time-consuming compared to case-control studies?

options.text: Longitudinal studies require matching more variables than case-control studies
Longitudinal studies must follow participants forward over prolonged periods, requiring sustained funding and monitoring of attrition
Longitudinal studies cannot use hospital or clinic records for data collection
Longitudinal studies require double-blind methodology not needed for case-control studies
Longitudinal studies must recruit participants from multiple countries

correct_answer.text: Longitudinal studies must follow participants forward over prolonged periods, requiring sustained funding and monitoring of attrition

questions.explanation: Prospective longitudinal studies follow the same cohort over extended timeframes, requiring continuous funding, staff, and management of participant attrition and loss-to-follow-up. Case-control studies are retrospective and faster because outcomes have already occurred. Options A, C, D, and E misstate or don't address the core time and cost drivers. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher plans to investigate whether childhood trauma is associated with adult depression onset. Both exposure (trauma) and outcome (depression) have already occurred in potential study subjects. Which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Randomized controlled trial
Prospective cohort study starting today
Case-control study
Cross-sectional survey
Ecological study of trauma rates by region

correct_answer.text: Case-control study

questions.explanation: Since both exposure and outcome have already occurred, a retrospective case-control study is most appropriate and efficient. Researchers identify depressed cases and non-depressed controls, then retrospectively assess childhood trauma exposure in both groups. Option A is inappropriate for observational questions. Option B would be inefficient (waiting for new outcomes). Options D and E don't directly address the causal question. ---

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of treatment side effects, four controls are matched to each case. If the researcher wishes to further increase statistical power by recruiting more controls, what would be the next logical step?

options.text: Recruit 8 controls per case (2:1 ratio)
Recruit controls up to a maximum of 4:1 ratio, beyond which power gains are minimal
Increase to 5 controls per case
Reduce the number of cases to maintain optimal sample proportions
Stop recruitment as power is already maximized at 1:4 ratio

Four controls per case is already at the optimal point, so recruiting beyond this ratio would waste resources without meaningful power gain. Options A and C suggest exceeding the optimal ratio. Options D and E misunderstand the dose-response relationship between control number and power. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher suspects that a medication causes a rare adverse psychiatric outcome. Which study design should be employed first to investigate this suspected association?

options.text: Prospective cohort study enrolling 10,000 participants
Case-control study of affected individuals and unaffected controls
Cross-sectional prevalence survey
Randomized controlled trial
Ecological study of medication use by country

questions.explanation: For rare diseases or outcomes, case-control studies are the most efficient first-line analytical approach because researchers can directly recruit affected individuals rather than waiting for rare events to occur in a prospective cohort. The source explicitly notes case-control studies are often the first mode of studying a suspected association. Option A is inefficient for rare outcomes. Options C, D, and E are unsuitable for investigating suspected causality in rare conditions. ---

questions.question_text: A retrospective study assembles subjects based on disease status and then collects historical exposure data. This design is most suitable for investigating which type of disease?

options.text: Common diseases with long latency periods
Rare diseases with clear diagnostic criteria
Diseases requiring long-term follow-up data

Outcomes requiring prospective observation

questions.question_text: A census conducted in a psychiatric hospital documents all patients' diagnoses, medications, and symptom severity on a single day. This represents which study design category?

options.text: Longitudinal analytical study
Experimental study
Cross-sectional descriptive study
Prospective cohort study
Case-control study

questions.question_text: A study compares the prevalence of anxiety disorders across three different occupational groups measured at a single point in time. Which statement best describes this study?

questions.question_text: A psychiatric epidemiologist studies whether unemployment precedes depression onset or depression leads to unemployment loss. Which study design is most appropriate?

Case-control study
Prospective cohort study
Ecological study
Case series

questions.question_text: A study identifies individuals who abuse alcohol and compares their childhood trauma history to non-abusing controls. This is an example of which study design?

options.text: Prospective cohort study
Case-control study
Experimental study
Cross-sectional survey
Ecological study

questions.question_text: When matching controls to cases in a case-control study, overzealous matching can result in which unintended consequence?

questions.question_text: A census of all mental health patients in a region is an example of which type of study?

Cross-sectional study

Cohort study
Case-control study

questions.question_text: A case-control study of medication adverse events matches cases and controls on age and sex but finds that the matched variables are actually strongly associated with exposure to the medication. What consequence might this create?

questions.question_text: Ecological studies consider which of the following as the unit of measurement?

Populations rather than individuals
Randomly selected cases and controls
Prospectively followed cohorts

questions.question_text: In a case-control study, the ratio of controls to cases is increased from 2:1 to 5:1. According to the source material, what is the expected effect on study power?

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of personality disorders and childhood trauma, strict diagnostic criteria for personality disorder cases serve which function?

questions.question_text: In a case-control study examining the relationship between childhood trauma and adult depression, which statement about the temporal sequence is most accurate?

The study proves causality through temporal relationships

questions.question_text: A cross-sectional study finds that individuals with depression have lower education levels than those without depression. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist notes that in their outpatient clinic, anxiety disorders are more common in female patients than males and wants to understand population-level prevalence. Which study design should they use?

options.text: Experimental trial comparing treatment outcomes

Cross-sectional population survey
Prospective cohort study
Ecological analysis of clinic data

questions.question_text: A prospective cohort study initially enrolled 1,000 participants but only 600 completed the full 10-year follow-up period. How might this attrition affect interpretation of results?

options.text: Attrition cannot occur in prospective studies by definition
Attrition is irrelevant if the original sample size was large

questions.question_text: A diagnostic assessment study comparing a new psychiatric screening tool to a gold standard should use which design?

options.text: Case-control study
Cohort study
Cross-sectional comparison to gold standard
Ecological study
Prospective randomized trial

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of psychiatric medication side effects, exposure information is collected by asking patients to recall their medication use 5 years ago. What bias is most likely to affect this study?

Recall bias

Ecological fallacy
Matching bias

questions.question_text: A prospective cohort study follows 500 individuals exposed to a psychosocial stressor and 500 unexposed individuals for 10 years, assessing anxiety disorder development. Why might this design be preferred over a case-control approach for studying this risk factor?

options.text: Cohort studies are cheaper than case-control studies
Cohort studies directly establish temporal sequence and can measure both incidence and relative risk
Cohort studies eliminate the possibility of confounding variables
Cohort studies require less time than case-control studies
Cohort studies can measure odds ratio more accurately

questions.question_text: Matching in case-control studies serves which primary purpose?

options.text: To eliminate all sources of bias in the study
To ensure comparability and control for confounding by selected variables

To guarantee statistical significance
To establish causality between exposure and outcome

questions.question_text: A mental health survey collects data on depression symptoms and self-reported childhood abuse in 5,000 community residents at a single time point. Which statement best describes what this study can determine?

The association between childhood abuse and depression at that time point

The temporal sequence of abuse and depression onset

questions.question_text: When selecting controls in a case-control study, hospital patients with a different health problem than cases are chosen. Which advantage does this approach provide?

questions.question_text: What is the ecological fallacy?

Drawing subject-level conclusions based on group-level observations
Failing to match cases and controls on key variables
Recruiting controls independent of exposure status
Measuring both exposure and outcome at the same time point

questions.question_text: An experimental study randomizes patients to receive either a new psychotherapy intervention or treatment-as-usual, measuring symptom change at 12 weeks. What is the relationship between this design and causal inference?

Randomization minimizes selection bias and confounding, supporting causal inference

questions.question_text: A longitudinal cohort study following individuals over 10 years to identify risk factors for developing schizophrenia would measure:

questions.question_text: A study measures depression prevalence among healthcare workers at a single timepoint in December 2024. Which study design is this?
